topics.name: Variables
topics.explanation: A variable is a name used to store data in memory so it can be reused later in a program. Python does not require you to declare a type — it is inferred automatically.
common_mistakes: Using a variable before assigning it a value
Using Python keywords (like 'class' or 'print') as variable names
Confusing '=' (assignment) with '==' (comparison)
topics.practice_tip: Try creating variables for your name, age, and favorite color, then print them together in one sentence.

topics.name: Data Types
topics.explanation: Python has built-in data types such as int (whole numbers), float (decimals), str (text), and bool (True/False).
topics.example:
x = 10        # int
y = 3.14      # float
name = "Sam"   # str
is_valid = True # bool
common_mistakes: Trying to add a string and a number directly (e.g. "Age: " + 20 causes an error)
Forgetting quotes around strings
topics.practice_tip: Use type() on different variables to see what data type Python assigns them.

topics.name: If-Elif-Else
topics.explanation: Conditional statements let your program make decisions and run different code blocks depending on whether a condition is True or False.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the colon ':' at the end of if/elif/else lines
Incorrect indentation inside the if block
Using '=' instead of '==' in the condition
topics.practice_tip: Write a program that checks if a number is positive, negative, or zero.

topics.name: Loops
topics.explanation: Loops let you repeat a block of code multiple times. A 'for' loop is used when you know how many times to repeat, and a 'while' loop is used when repetition depends on a condition.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to update the loop variable in a while loop, causing an infinite loop
Off-by-one errors with range()
Incorrect indentation inside the loop body
topics.practice_tip: Write a loop that prints the multiplication table of 5.

topics.name: Functions
topics.explanation: A function is a reusable block of code that performs a specific task. You define it once using 'def' and can call it many times.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to use 'return' when a value needs to be sent back
Mismatched number of arguments when calling the function
Forgetting parentheses when calling the function
topics.practice_tip: Write a function that takes two numbers and returns their sum.

topics.name: Lists
topics.explanation: A list is an ordered, changeable collection used to store multiple items in a single variable, written with square brackets.
common_mistakes: Index out of range errors (e.g. accessing fruits[10] on a 3-item list)
Forgetting that list indexing starts at 0, not 1
topics.practice_tip: Create a list of your 3 favorite movies and print each one using a loop.

topics.name: Dictionaries
topics.explanation: A dictionary stores data as key-value pairs, useful for looking up values quickly using a key instead of a numeric index.
common_mistakes: Trying to access a key that doesn't exist (causes KeyError)
Confusing dictionaries { } with lists [ ]
topics.practice_tip: Create a dictionary storing your name, age, and course, then print each value.

topics.name: Common Errors
topics.explanation: Beginners often run into a few common Python errors: SyntaxError (typos or missing punctuation), IndentationError (incorrect spacing), NameError (using an undefined variable), and TypeError (mixing incompatible data types).
common_mistakes: Not reading the error message carefully — it usually tells you the exact line and reason
Ignoring indentation consistency (mixing tabs and spaces)
topics.practice_tip: When you get an error, read the last line of the traceback first — it names the error type and often the fix.

topics.name: String Operations
topics.explanation: Strings are sequences of characters. Python provides many built-in methods to work with them, like .upper(), .lower(), .split(), and .format().
common_mistakes: Forgetting that strings are immutable — methods return a new string rather than changing the original
Mixing up single and double quotes inconsistently
topics.practice_tip: Take a sentence and try reversing it, counting its words, and converting it to uppercase.
